data.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference
data.summary:
The application referenced records by identifiers supplied in the request without
verifying that the authenticated user was entitled to access them, allowing any
user to retrieve and modify other users' data.
data.description:
The application identified records through values carried in the request, such as
a numeric record identifier in a URL path or a query parameter. Authentication
was enforced correctly, but no authorisation check was performed to confirm that
the record requested belonged to the authenticated user or fell within the scope
of their role.

As a result, any authenticated user could access any record simply by altering
the identifier. Where identifiers were sequential, the full data set could be
enumerated by incrementing the value; where they were less predictable, they
remained retrievable from other parts of the application that disclosed them
legitimately.

The same weakness applied to operations that modify state. Requests to update or
delete a record succeeded regardless of ownership, extending the impact beyond
disclosure to unauthorised modification.

Controls that conceal the affected functionality from the user interface provide
no protection, as the request is constructed directly rather than through the
interface.
data.impact:
Any authenticated user could retrieve, modify, or delete records belonging to
other users, including data classed as sensitive. Because the records are
enumerable, an attacker holding a single valid account could extract the
application's entire data set, and the ability to modify records without
authorisation undermines the integrity of the data the business relies upon.
data.recommendation:
1. Enforce an authorisation check on every request that references a record,
   verifying against the authenticated session that the user is entitled to the
   specific record and the specific operation requested.

2. Implement the check server side within the data access layer, so that it
   applies uniformly and cannot be omitted when new endpoints are added.

3. Scope queries to the authenticated user where the business model permits,
   retrieving records by owner and identifier together rather than by identifier
   alone, so that an unauthorised request returns nothing.

4. Replace sequential identifiers with values that cannot be guessed, as a
   defence-in-depth measure. This raises the effort required for enumeration but
   does not substitute for the authorisation check.

5. Include authorisation testing in the development process, covering each
   endpoint with a request issued by a user who should not have access.
